endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Throughout the AI tool’s lifecycle, the multidisciplinary development team shall analyse potential risks, assess each risk’s likelihood, effects and risk-benefit balance, define risk mitigation measures, monitor the risks and mitigations continuously, and maintain a risk management file.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Mitigate, transfer, or avoid risks that surpass organizational risk tolerances.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Integrating AI intake findings into contract negotiations: use identified risks or gaps in vendor documentation to inform specific contract requirements.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: ID.SC-3: Contracts with suppliers and thirdparty partners are used to implement appropriate measures designed to meet the objectives of an organization’s cybersecurity program and Cyber Supply Chain Risk Management Plan.

endorsements.title: Integrating enterprise risk management to address AI-related risks in healthcare: Strategies for effective risk mitigation and implementation
endorsements.issuer: Journal of healthcare risk management : the journal of the American Society for Healthcare Risk Management
endorsements.quote: ERM offers various risk control techniques to address AI‐related risks, such as risk control (limiting AI use in clinically sensitive areas), risk reduction (introducing backup systems and manual checks), and risk transfer (insurance against AI‐related errors or damage from cyberattacks).

evidence.title: Experimental investigation of real-time 3D beam's eye view image-guided radiotherapy for prostate SBRT
evidence.effect: Mitigation strategies including eligibility screening, staff training, and workflow formalization reduced average RPN by 43% across the top ten high-risk failure modes.
evidence.quote: Incorporation of mitigation strategies-including eligibility screening, staff training, and workflow formalization-resulted in an average RPN reduction of 43% across the top ten high-risk failure modes.
evidence.sample_unit: phantom experimental tests (static and dynamic, four patient-derived motion traces)

commentary.bottom_line: Five guidance and framework sources endorse documenting a mitigate, transfer, avoid, or accept response for each identified AI risk, but only one simulated phantom study tests any part of it and reports a 43% average reduction in risk priority scores after mitigation. No study tests the transfer, avoid, or accept options, or whether documented responses change patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: One level 4 study using 25 phantom tests in an offline setting reports that mitigation lowered the average risk priority number by 43% across ten high-risk failure modes. The design is simulated, the clinical setting is not reported, and the outcome is a scored risk estimate rather than observed harm. Certainty is very low for indirectness and imprecision.

Eligibility screening, staff training, and workflow formalization were the mitigations applied to the top ten failure modes, and their scored risk fell by 43% on average. Risk priority numbers depend on team judgment of severity, occurrence, and detection, so the reduction may reflect rescoring as much as fewer errors reaching patients.

The mitigations in the single study were workflow and training changes, which suggests that risk responses are carried out inside clinical routines rather than in the model. The study used phantoms and motion traces, so it does not show whether staff sustain these steps in live care or what time they require.

FUTURE-AI states that teams shall maintain a risk management file, and NIST AI 600-1 advises mitigating, transferring, or avoiding risks above organizational tolerance. CHAI sources describe using contracts to assign risk to vendors. These endorsements rest on consensus and existing risk-management practice, and no supplied study tests contractual transfer or documented acceptance.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares governance programs that document a response for each AI risk with programs that do not, and none examines transfer through contracts or insurance, avoidance, or formal acceptance. Prospective studies in deployed clinical settings should measure observed errors and harms in addition to risk priority scores, and they should report staff time and cost.
commentary.underserved_note: The one test used phantoms and patient-derived motion traces and reported no patient population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from this evidence whether risk scoring and chosen responses account for hazards that fall more heavily on these groups.
